property_summary: For any deposit value and sender, calling receive() on the correct contract always makes depositsCount non-decreasing (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant using unchecked++ can wrap and make depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some inputs.

For any sender and any amount, a call to receive() on the correct contract never decreases depositsCount (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant uses unchecked++ so wrapping can make depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some inputs.

For any initial depositsCount and any sequence of calls to receive driven by a single caller sending arbitrary amounts, the correct contract's depositsCount increases by exactly the number of receive calls (i.e., depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + nCalls); the mutant can wrap on overflow so there exist inputs (initial depositsCount and number of calls) where depositsCount_after != depositsCount_before + nCalls.

For every single receive call, the correct contract's depositsCount after the call is equal to depositsCount before the call plus one (i.e., it never wraps), whereas the mutant with unchecked increment can wrap so there exist starting depositsCount values for which a single receive call makes depositsCount_after != depositsCount_before + 1.

For any caller and any amount, a single receive call on the correct contract always leaves depositsCount >= previous value (non-decreasing); the mutant's unchecked increment can wrap depositsCount and make it smaller for some initial depositsCount values, violating this rule.

For any payable send to receive(), the reference contract guarantees that depositsCount only increases when the call does not revert (i.e., the require prevents state change on failure), whereas the mutant unconditionally increments depositsCount even when the external transfer would have reverted, allowing depositsCount to increase despite a failing external condition.

For any incoming payable call, the reference contract C ensures that depositsCount increases only if the call completes successfully (i.e., no revert from the receiver path); the mutant increments depositsCount unconditionally, so there exist inputs (a sender that causes the call to revert) where depositsCount increases in the mutant but the reference preserves that it did not increase on reverted calls.

For any external caller and any sent ETH amount, a successful receive call on the reference C always increments depositsCount by 1 and leaves it unchanged when the call reverts; the mutant increments unconditionally, so there exists a caller (a reverter) and amount for which the mutant's depositsCount increases despite the call reverting while the reference's does not.

For any caller and any sent ETH amount, calling C.receive succeeds (does not revert) exactly when the receiver's fallback/receive does not revert; the reference contract's depositsCount only increases when the call returns successfully, while the mutant increments depositsCount even if an external receiver reverts — so there exists a callee (a reverter helper used as the msg.sender via vm.prank) and amount for which the mutant's depositsCount increases despite the call reverting, violating the reference rule.

For every payable call to C (its receive), the correct contract only increments depositsCount when the call completes successfully (no revert); the mutant increments depositsCount even when the call would revert, so there exist inputs (an adversarial receiving address that reverts and some sent value) that make the mutant's depositsCount increase while the reference's does not.

For any nonnegative ether amount sent to C via its receive() by any sender, depositsCount increases by 1 (receive accepts and increments); the mutant that unconditionally reverts breaks this because receive() will revert and depositsCount will not increase for some send amounts/senders.

For any externally-sent nonzero ether deposit to C, the reference contract always accepts the payment and increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount increases after a successful receive), whereas the mutant that unconditionally reverts breaks this by reverting the receive and thus not increasing depositsCount (and causing the call to fail) for some inputs.

For any sender and any nonzero ETH amount sent to C via its receive(), the reference contract always accepts the payment (call succeeds) and increments depositsCount by 1; the mutant that unconditionally reverts will cause the receive call to fail (revert) for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For any sender and any nonzero ETH amount sent to C via its receive(), the reference contract always accepts the payment (call succeeds) and increments depositsCount by 1 (so a send succeeds and depositsCount increases), whereas the mutant that unconditionally reverts will cause the receive call to fail (revert) for some inputs, breaking this rule.

For any caller and any nonnegative deposit amount, sending ETH to C via its receive() always increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant's stricter require can revert for some input (specifically when arithmetic flags differ at the overflow edge), breaking this rule.

For any sender and any nonnegative ETH amount that the sender can send, calling receive() always succeeds and increases depositsCount by exactly 1 in the reference; the mutant's stricter require can revert for some input (specifically when addition would wrap under 0xFFFFFFFF... edge conditions), so the mutant can make the receive call fail for some fuzzed amounts.

For any sender and any nonnegative ETH amount they send, a successful call to C.receive always increases depositsCount by exactly 1 (i.e. depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant's stricter require can cause receive to revert for some deposit values (e.g. edgecases around uint overflow), so the mutant will fail this property for some fuzzed amounts.

For any sender and any nonnegative ETH amount they send, if the receive call succeeds then C.depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant's stricter require can make receive revert for some inputs so the increment does not occur for those inputs.

For any sender and any nonnegative ETH amount they can send, a successful call to C.receive always increases depositsCount by exactly 1 (depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant's stricter require can make receive revert for certain deposit values so this relation can fail.

For any payable call to receive with any caller and any nonnegative ether value, the reference contract always leaves depositsCount non-decreasing by exactly 1 (i.e., depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1) while the mutant that increments before checking can revert during execution and thus can cause a failed call (revert) for some inputs where the reference would succeed, producing a mismatch in final depositsCount and success status.

For any caller and any payable amount, calling receive should never revert and should always increase depositsCount by 1 (so the call succeeds); the mutant that increments before checking can cause a revert for some inputs, making the call fail.

For every caller and nonnegative ether value, calling the reference contract's receive() always succeeds and increases depositsCount by exactly 1 (so the call returns true / does not revert and depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant that increments before the require can revert for some inputs causing the call to fail (revert) and not produce that net increment.

For any caller and any nonnegative ether value, calling receive() on the correct contract always succeeds (does not revert) and increases depositsCount by exactly 1; the mutant that increments before the require can revert during execution for some inputs (due to arithmetic underflow in the checked expression context) causing the call to fail and breaking this rule.

For any caller and any nonnegative ether value, calling the reference contract's receive() never reverts and therefore always increases depositsCount by exactly 1; the mutant that increments before the require can cause the call to revert for some inputs (transiently leaving state unchanged), so there exist inputs where the mutant's call fails while the reference's call succeeds.

property_summary: A call to withdrawAll reverts for any caller who is not the contract owner.
Calls to withdrawAll revert for any caller that is not the contract owner.
For any caller address different from the contract owner, calling withdrawAll must revert (i.e., withdrawAll is owner-only).

For any caller who is owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll always invokes C.withdraw(uint) so that any callee-side logic (e.g., a reverter in withdraw) can affect outcome; the mutant that replaces the call with an inline transfer bypasses withdraw(...) and therefore cannot observe/propagate withdraw's behavior (e.g. a failing/reverting override) — this test uses a malicious override that reverts in withdraw to differentiate them.

For any caller and any balance, if the contract's withdraw(uint) function reverts when invoked on a malicious override, then calling withdrawAll() on the reference C (which routes to withdraw) will propagate that revert (so the call reverts), while the mutant that does an inline transfer will not invoke withdraw and therefore will not revert — i.e., withdrawAll() should revert whenever withdraw(uint) reverts, but the mutant can succeed for some inputs.

For all callers and contract balances, C.withdrawAll() always forwards its operation through the contract's withdraw(uint) entry (so any behavior of withdraw — including reverts from an overriding malicious contract — is observed), whereas the mutant that inlines a direct transfer can succeed while withdraw would have reverted; hence the property: calling withdrawAll() will revert exactly when withdraw(uint) would revert for the same caller and balance.

For any caller (owner) and any contract balance, C.withdrawAll() always delegates to withdraw(uint) so it reverts whenever an overriding withdraw(uint) would revert; the mutant inlines transfer and can succeed for some inputs where withdraw(uint) (overridden to revert) would cause withdrawAll() to revert.

For any caller and any balance, C.withdrawAll() always invokes the contract's withdraw(uint) and thus will revert if an overriding withdraw(uint) reverts; the mutant that inlines a direct transfer breaks this by succeeding for some inputs where withdraw(uint) would revert.
When the contract holds a positive ETH balance and owner withdraws the full amount, the withdrawal call always succeeds (does not revert) and reduces the contract balance to zero.
A call to withdraw by the contract owner never reverts (i.e., withdraw always succeeds) for any withdrawal amount when invoked through c.withdraw(...).
Calling c.withdraw(amount) in run should not revert (i.e., the call must succeed).
The test asserts that calling c.withdraw(amount) does not revert (i.e., the call succeeds).
The test asserts that calling c.withdraw(amount) does not revert (i.e., the call succeeds).

For any callee that reverts when receiving Ether, the reference contract C's sendMoney call will NOT change C's withdraw behavior (owner can still withdraw the contract balance), but the mutated version that uses low-level call+require in withdraw will revert/behave differently after such a failed external send, causing withdraw to fail for some inputs.

For any target address and value, if the contract has positive balance equal to value then the reference contract C always allows the owner to withdraw that balance (withdraw succeeds), whereas the mutant that uses call+require in withdraw can fail to withdraw if the owner is a contract whose fallback consumes gas / causes call to fail — so there exists a target (a reverting receiver used earlier) that makes withdraw revert in the mutant but not in the reference.

For any target callee and value, after sending money via sendMoney the contract's owner can always withdraw the contract's full balance (reference holds); the mutant that switches to a low-level call+require in withdraw can fail to withdraw when the owner's receiving call fails, breaking this property for some inputs.
